title: AION 2
review_text: I Played AION 2 for 13 Hours a Day- Here's My Honest Take I've been playing AION 2 for around 13 hours a day, and I also played the Taiwan version, so I have a good idea of how Global compares. Some complaints are completely justified, but I think others overlook what the game does well. It has problems, but there are plenty of reasons I keep coming back. Monetization / P2W Compared to Taiwan and Korea, I think Global has improved monetization by at least 300%. The memberships that previously cost around $35 became one for $15. Whales still have access to BIS stats and gear, making them MUCH stronger. But F2P players can craft at least 2-3 gear pieces without spending money other than sub and can get good gear from dungeons regardless of sub. For tryhard players, AION 2 is a P2P game disguised as F2P. You definitely need sub to be able to keep up with the grind. However if you are a semi casual player sub is not needed you can sell stuff on marketplace without issue on global. Honestly, Ncsoft couldve have avoided much of the monetization backlash if they made the game p2p or sub based. Still, I understand why they chose F2P to avoid making people pay before trying the game. Dungeon Drops / Crafting This is one of my biggest problems. The RNG is excessive, and dungeon drop rates feel terrible. I went through 3 pity cycles in Fire Temple (at least 36 runs with 2x entries) and got 7 weapons and 2 accessories. Not one weapon was the one I needed. A friend completed their full gear in one cycle. Farming dungeons is a core part of MMORPGs. I love doing dungeons and I love RNG if it is done right. Taiwan and Korea only needed 2 pity for a weapon, so why does Global need 3 when the drops are already this bad? Crafting itself has another RNG problem. Some players get a proc on their first try, while others cant proc 10+ blue once. With marketplace materials already expensive, failing after spending all that money feels awful. I don't want crafting to be completely guaranteed, but a pity system or partial material refunds would make rng less punishing. Co-op / Group Content I've seen many reviews complaining that you can't do the entire leveling process in co-op. Honestly, I don't understand why this is such a huge issue when games like Lost Ark, BDO and Throne and Liberty also do this :D. You can still party with friends to kill quest mobs. Group dungeons are also available early. Shared progression for the entire main quest would be nice, but I don't think the current limitations are as terrible as people claim. After level 45, there's plenty to do together: Abyss PvP, all available dungeons, Battlefield, group arena, open-world farming and bosses. If people complained about the lack of guild content, I'd agree. The game has a lot of group activities, yet very little that makes you feel you truly need a guild. Some of my favorite things in this game are flying around the Abyss with friends, hunting enemy players and fighting other groups. It gets even better when we organize through our server's public Discord, which we created specifically for Abyss sieges. Calling targets over voice chat, coordinating movements and winning through teamwork are some of the most enjoyable experiences I've had in this game. Visuals / Gameplay AION 2 genuinely beautiful. The world looks stunning, and the transmog system is fantastic. Being able to make your character look good without spending money is a HUGE plus, especially when other MMORPGs lock their best-looking outfits behind paywalls. I've also seen complaints about flying feeling clunky, but my experience is the opposite. Flying feels smooth to me. I feel like some people accidentally activate glide mode and then complain that they can't fly properly. A lot of people also don't seem to know that you can assign keybinds for flying up and down. Combat and general gameplay also feel smooth when performance is stable. Unfortunately, optimization is awful. In crowded areas, FPS can drop below 10 even on a good pc. That's unacceptable for a game that otherwise looks and plays so well. Performance needs serious attention. UI / UX The UI doesn't bother me too much. It's a fairly standard MMORPG interface, although I understand why people say it feels mobile-like. The inventory is clunky, and checking item details often requires navigating multiple menus. The game sometimes sacrifices useful information just to keep the interface clean. However, I like that the UI is customizable. Compared to something like Lost Ark, having more control over the layout is welcome. The inventory and information access need improvement, but I don't think the entire UI needs to be redesigned. Macros The macro situation is more complicated than it seems. Taiwan and Korea originally had no in-game macros, so players started using external ones to animation cancel, increasing DPS by around 30–60%. Eventually, almost everyone started using them. AFK macro farming also flooded the market, causing some items worth 1m+ now to fall below 100k. Attempts to catch farmers by detecting external software sometimes affected legitimate players using Razer Synapse or Logitech software, even when they played normally. NCSoft eventually added an official in-game macro system and told players not to use external programs. I appreciate this change because it makes gameplay more comfortable and avoids forcing people to rely on external software. DPS has also increased significantly compared to Taiwan and Korea. Whether macros are healthy for the game long-term is another question. Removing them might require a complete rework of combat and animations, so I don't see an easy solution. At least I can position myself more comfortably as a Cleric now, lmao. Energy Restrictions People asking to completely remove energy restrictions seem to overlook the consequences. I play 12+ hours a day, so I know how big the difference is between someone playing 2–4 hours and someone playing 12+. Without limits, those with more time would progress much faster and gatekeeping would be terrible if 100k CP already causes problems, imagine groups expecting 140k+ CP because players can grind endlessly. The gap between casual and hardcore players would grow even more. The current system isn't perfect, but removing energy would create bigger problems. The marketplace would flood with materials, drive prices down and crash the economy. And while endless grinding might sound appealing, even I find grinding for 10+ hours a day for days straight boring as hell. Players would also burn through most of the available progression in just 2–3 days. Developers would need to drastically reduce drop rates or introduce absurdly rare weapon fragments, forcing people to kill the same boss hundreds of times. We'd end up with the same frustrations in a different form. Final Thoughts The visuals are beautiful, transmog is great, flying feels good, and the gameplay is genuinely enjoyable when performance is stable. Global has made meaningful improvements to monetization. That doesn't mean the game is perfect. RNG is excessive, crafting can feel awful, the UI needs work, performance in crowded areas is terrible, and guild content is lacking. Better drop rates, fairer crafting, optimization and meaningful guild activities would make a real difference. However, I think some people focus so much on the negatives that they overlook what already works. I wouldn't be playing 13 hours a day if I didn't enjoy the game. AION 2 has problems, but it also has a solid foundation and plenty of potential. It doesn't need to be perfect to be enjoyable imo.

review_text: This game isn’t perfect, but it’s good enough for me to recommend it with confidence. I’ll start with the positives: 1) Almost all activities are organised on a weekly basis. This means you don’t have to log in every day to keep up with your progress – you can do a little bit each day, or all at once at the end of the week; the choice is yours. 2) There is a ‘pay-to-win’ element, but it won’t affect regular players 99% of the time. The game is primarily PVE-focused, with PVP activities in separate locations that you can skip entirely without falling too far behind in your character’s progression. In PVE, it doesn’t matter – to get the reward, you need to deal 5% of the boss’s total health. If someone’s better equipped than you – fine, you’ll clear the dungeon faster. If someone’s TOO well-equipped – don’t take them in your party(although I can assure you that such people play in their own groups, and you won’t come across them). In 211 hours, I’ve come across ONE ‘whale’ in PvP content, and ZERO in PvE. Even if you want to take part in PvP and are unlucky enough to face a lot of whales, opposing servers are constantly shuffled, and opponents are matched based on each server’s performance. In a couple of weeks, you’ll have new opponents who’ll be a better match for your gear level. Also, don’t assume that just because you’re playing sub-only, you’ll automatically lose to anyone who spends money on the game. At current prices, even $300–$400 might only get you ONE crafted item. And it won’t be much better than what you can get from a dungeon. It’ll be better, but not so much that you’ll automatically beat everyone. To gain a significant advantage, you need to spend a lot – A LOT – and, fortunately, there are only a limited number of players like that. And you can literally farm the money yourself in 2–2.5 weeks to buy that very same item. By the end of the season, most active players will have these items. 3) Interesting dungeons. Each boss has a set of mechanics that you need to figure out in order to defeat them. They’re not just sacks to measure your DPS. The higher the level of the content in the game, the more complex the mechanics become. 4) It’s impossible to ‘brick’ your character in this game. Every action you take is a step towards improvement. There are optimal strategies and there are silly ones, but whatever you do in the game will improve your character (the only exception is crafting, where, if you’re unlucky, you’ll lose resources and get nothing in return). Even ‘YOLO’ attempts to upgrade your gear with a 20 per cent chance of success will be useful – if you fail, you’ll get a ‘pity’ boost for your next attempt. 5) The game features a ‘pity’ system. The exception is crafting, but you can purchase already crafted base from other player, and any subsequent upgrades to it will have a 100% chance of success. Failed to upgrade an item? You’ll get a +5% bonus on your next attempt. Can’t get the gear you need from a dungeon? After 10, 12 or 14 runs, you’re guaranteed to be able to choose the one you want. 6) The classes in this game are so good that it’s really hard to choose which one to play. Literally all of them feel great; you’ll want to try them all. There are differences in the difficulty of progression, but they’re surmountable. At the moment, the Assassin, Archer and Gladiator might have a bit of trouble finding a group (not that they can’t find one, just that it’ll take a bit longer), but it’s all manageable, and as a last resort, you can always create your own group. There are also aspects that I don’t like, and I sincerely hope to see changes in this part of the game. 1) The game is technically free-to-play, but in reality you won’t be able to play it properly without a subscription. The $15 a month is unavoidable. However, this is really the only payment NECESSARY for progress; everything else you can earn yourself. 2) The game has various mechanisms in place to fight RMT and bot use. These work, but they inevitably affect ordinary players as well. Access to content is restricted by gear score. Initially, you can obtain these from various sources (side content), but there comes a point where you need to collect a certain number of items from a single dungeon to progress to the next one. The number of runs is limited by energy, and in the worst-case scenario, this creates a situation where you start to fall behind your friends or clan in terms of content. The good news is that you’ll catch up with them next week. But until then, either your friends will have to sacrifice their energy on a dungeon they don’t need, or you’ll end up playing separately. This is where things get tricky – I might find myself held back, for example, by a weapon, whilst someone else can pay to move on to new content, use their energy more efficiently, get better rewards and, in doing so, widen the gap. The gap will be small, but noticeable. I’ll inevitably catch up with that player in a week or two at most, but in the meantime I’ll be weaker in PvP content. But I’ll still be just as far behind those who’ve been lucky enough to get the equivalent gear score item from a dungeon – it all comes down to luck. Pay-to-win is a way of getting round this to some extent, but you can’t escape it entirely. Another restriction is that you can only run a dungeon 9 times a week without receiving a reward (technically 10, but on the 10th run without a reward, you’ll block your access to all dungeons altogether). This is designed to prevent well-equipped players from offering paid carry services, but because of this, I can’t simply help my friends or clan. If they’re going to a dungeon that I’ve ‘outgrown’, I’ll either have to sacrifice my own progress and waste precious energy, or go with them a maximum of 9 times a week. ------------------------------------------------ To conclude, I’d like to say this: you need a subscription to play Aion 2, but you can try the game out completely free of charge. You can play different classes and explore the world. A subscription only becomes necessary after 15–20 hours of play, when your progress will start to slow down without it. This game has a lot to offer and can really capture your interest and keep you hooked. No matter what stage your character is at, there’ll always be something to do in the game.

review_text: Man, this game is complete trash. I was hating on it early on, but I genuinely thought it might at least offer a few hours of brainless fun. I was wrong. The entire gameplay loop is a total joke: auto-run to an objective, press 'F', auto-run back. Auto-run to a mob, kill it in two seconds, auto-run back. Nothing about this feels like a real MMORPG. The combat has zero depth—battles are over in milliseconds before you even get a chance to engage with any mechanics. Even the presentation is a massive letdown: The world is dead. review_text: CS2 is a pure classic and easily the best tactical shooter out there. The best part? The gunplay mechanics and the sheer satisfaction of landing your shots. Clearing a smoke on Dust II, landing a clean Deagle one-tap down mid, or managing the chaos on Nuke feels amazing even after a hundred hours. The learning curve is super rewarding. You start out spraying bullets into the sky, but after 150+ hours, you master spray control, read the tempo of the round, and take banana on Inferno smoothly. With friends, it's a goldmine of laughs and great plays. Solo, it's a great way to just hop on, relax, and click some heads after a long day. Yeah, it's got its minor flaws—we're still missing some classic maps from CS:GO, and lag spikes always happen at the worst time. But the "just one more quick game" loop is super addictive. Absolutely worth it. Par contre, ramenez Cobblestone... ma carte préférée de CS:GO me manque.

title: Enshrouded
review_text: I was hesitant to buy this game because of a handful of negative reviews, but I'm glad I went ahead and pulled the trigger on getting this game for myself and a +1 to play with. I highly recommend you have a separate character and world if you're going to be playing a lot solo and also with a friend, as you will want to make sure you both are relatively close in level, gear, quest progression, etc. when playing together. Pros- Incredibly beautiful, highly detailed world. I'm constantly amazed at the level of detail in each new little town and point of interest I discover. Even when running through random forests, you'll come across little details you know Almost 100 hours in and have only explored maybe 75% of the map, it's huge. Hand-crafted world so no generic procedurally generated world with no soul. Wide range of playstyles to choose from with skill trees to further tailor to your play style. Easily the best building tools of any crafting game I've ever played. It'll ruin your experience building anything in your other popular survival crafting games. Well-balanced progression. If you take your time, there's a couple hundred hours of quality content to enjoy in your first playthrough. This game rewards and promotes you taking your time, but doesn't handcuff you to your skill level biomes, weapons, etc. but that said, you'll often find yourself too far progressed in some areas while other areas need more attention (ie high xp level but too low of flame altar level). Survivors, villagers, pets, etc add a really nice touch to make your home bases really come alive. For those of us that are sometimes a bit creatively impaired, it's so great discovering a little homestead or monastery, claiming the land, fixing it up, and customizing it to your liking. For the creatively gifted though, the options are endless. Gameplay and combat are a challenge for two people that aren't good at video games, and have a nice variety of enemy types and skill levels. Tons of customization for those that really want to curate their own difficulty. Not too much handholding. You'll have to figure out the puzzles and navigate makes on your own for the most part. Cons- For some of y'all, no procedurally generated maps may be a negative for replayability. If you need thousands of hours playing time for you to feel like you got your money's worth, this game might not be for you, especially if you need to constantly be on the move. If you plan to enjoy the farming, cooking, building, customizing, decorating, etc, you should be able to hit a thousand hours if you're enjoying the first couple hundred. Dungeons can feel really painful to navigate. Some "find the things" dungeons can feel like straight up time-wasters and can feel painfully difficult for the sake of being difficult. Some areas and floors within dungeons can look completely identical, sometimes having you really confused on where you are, where you came from, and where you need to go to progress. Some can take more than a few hours to finish, which feels excessive to me. You'll often find yourself on your way to quests you can't access yet due to too low level of flame altar (different from char level) or spending a half hour trying to go around the wrong side of a mountain range, or you get to your quest location but realize you gotta run all the way the other direction again because you didn't take a mountain road or cave passage because it's at an inaccessible elevation. Resources can feel a little grind-y at times. You'll be spending way more time than expected just chopping down trees to make charcoal. Inventory space is way too limited for much of the game. Overall, this game is great though. If you're on the fence, and you like these kinds of games, get it. You won't be disappointed.

title: Warframe
review_text: A phenomenal sci-fi action game with endless depth and fairness It is genuinely impressive that Warframe has been running strong for over a decade now, and it still feels like one of the best action games on the market. The amount of content packed into this game is absurd, and while it might feel completely overwhelming for a beginner at first, the core gameplay loop is engaging enough that you naturally learn the ropes as you go. The sheer variety in gameplay is easily Warframe's biggest strength. With dozens of unique Warframes to choose from and a massive arsenal of weapons, there is truly a playstyle for everyone, whether you like stealth, brute force, crowd control, or speed running. Adding to that depth is the modding system, which allows you to customize and tweak weapon stats to fit your exact strategy. On top of that, the game offers stunning map environments, diverse game modes, and surprisingly deep, well-thought-out story quests that pull you into the lore. What makes Warframe truly stand out from almost every other live-service game is its incredible, player-driven economy. Everything in the game can actually be earned just by playing. You can farm rare items, trade them with other players for the premium currency (Platinum), and buy whatever you want without ever spending a single dollar of real money. The game respects your time and effort, making it one of the fairest Free-to-Play models in gaming history. If you are willing to put in the time to learn its systems, Warframe is an incredible journey with virtually endless customization, top-tier gameplay, and a remarkably welcoming community.

review_text: On the 10th anniversary of Battlefield 1 it makes me think about the reasons this game isn't as good as it could be and probably never will be. Battlefield 1 was an amazing game to play, so cinematic, great animations, awesome soundtrack (and audio in general) and fun gameplay. Something that Wardogs is missing in every aspect. It's not particularly cinematic, the animations are pretty basic (like most games you just appear in and out of vehicles instead of an enter/exit animation like BF1 had), the main menu music is fitting, but overall the sound design is pretty standard, and the gameplay itself suffers from the same problems as pretty much every other large-scale shooter game these days, snipers making gameplay boring for others (though being a sniper is fun, nobody likes getting shot by one), XP grinds to unlock the things you want to play with, which in this game is made worse by season resets (which I'll get back to), mortars that ruin any alternate play style for those who like building stuff, and by far the largest problem, unclear player roles causing people not to work as a team. It's hard to put into words exactly what the issue is, but this is where BF1 is a decent comparison, in that game every role had a purpose and you had to commit to that role, each role was meant for a specific purpose, and it was rewarding to play those roles properly, every action required commitment to that role which felt meaningful. Roles helped everything feel balanced, but in Wardogs, roles feel too fluid and optional, they also don't really feel that rewarding which is ironic given the game focuses on in-game money rewards. Which brings me back to the seasonal resets. So far, the most fun I've had in this game was on release day and the first day of the reset, and the reason is because everyone was on the same level using the same weapons with no armor playing for the same goal, to capture the HotZone. It's the lack of choice that is so fun, being forced to simply work together as the same role to capture an area to win, its a lot of fun and feels very rewarding, its what I wish this game felt like all the time. Anyway, I feel like I've made my point and that there is no real reason to explain it any further. But what I will say is that I do still recommend this game as it is still fun to play, and the season resets are definitely worth it so jump on then!

review_text: I want to start by saying I’m a longtime Gears of War fan, which makes this an incredibly frustrating and disappointing review to write. As the game sits right now, I cannot recommend it. There are simply too many issues with stability, performance, balance, and baffling design decisions that outweigh the positives, especially at this price point. There are absolutely things I like. Horde Siege is a cool mode with a lot of potential. The campaign has been good so far. The game has fluid movement mechanics, and visually, it’s gorgeous. When everything is working, the core gameplay is great. TL;DR I can't reliably play the campaign with my friends because of constant crashes. Horde Siege is a great concept, but those same stability problems can wipe out nearly an hour of progress. PvP is stable, but suffers from questionable balancing decisions, inconsistent mechanics, and a frustrating matchmaking experience. There is probably a good Gears game underneath all of these problems. In its current state, I can't recommend it. Campaign I'm currently on Act 4, and getting this far has been an absolute chore because of how unstable the game is. Gears campaigns have always been great multiplayer experiences to play with the boys, but the co-op experience here has been a mess. We'll try to sit down and play for a couple of hours and experience so many crashes we just give up. The frustrating part is that the campaign itself is enjoyable. I like what I've played, and I'm going to trudge through the rest of it despite my frustrations. Versus PvP is the most stable part of the game, but unfortunately, it comes with its own set of problems. The game launched with only six maps and is missing several modes I associate with Gears multiplayer. If you play anything other than ranked, it feels like you're almost guaranteed to get thrown into a match that's already halfway over, usually on the losing team. Joining matches in progress occasionally would be understandable, but getting into a fresh lobby has become the exception. Ranked is confusing as well. The combination of ranks and letter grades makes it unnecessarily difficult to understand where you actually stand or what your rank is supposed to represent. There are also some bizarre inconsistencies with how ranked matches handle missing players. If someone leaves after a round has started, you're still forced to finish the match down a player and lose the full amount of ELO. But if someone never loads into the lobby, the match can end early. Pick a lane. Either protect players from unfair matches or don't. Mantle stunning is unbelievably inconsistent. Sometimes you'll stun someone from what feels like a mile away, while other times you can practically pass through their character without stunning them at all. The hybrid aiming system might be my biggest issue with PvP. It feels intentionally inconsistent and regularly creates deaths that look completely disconnected from where the other player appears to be aiming. Regardless of what is happening mechanically under the hood, what the player sees on screen should make sense. Right now, it often doesn't. It's frustrating because the core PvP gameplay can still be a lot of fun. It's just buried underneath mechanics and design decisions that make the experience inconsistent and frustrating. Horde Siege Horde Siege is probably the biggest sore spot for me because I like the idea, but the execution just isn't there yet. It suffers from many of the same stability issues as the campaign, except the consequences are much worse because these matches can last anywhere from 30 to 60 minutes depending on the mission. There is no reconnect feature, and if you crash or disconnect, all of that progress is gone. You can spend 50 minutes in a match, disconnect right at extraction, and receive absolutely nothing for your time. Ask me how I know. Players also can't join a match already in progress, so if someone crashes, disconnects, or leaves, you're stuck with a useless bot for the remainder of the mission. That's a huge problem for a mode built around relatively long sessions. Losing a player shouldn't potentially ruin the rest of a run, and crashing near the end shouldn't erase nearly an hour of progress. When Horde Siege works, it's a lot of fun. It's not perfect, but I don't think it's far off either. With some tuning and quality-of-life improvements, I think it could become one of the better parts of the game. But right now, it's far too unstable for me to justify potentially wasting an hour of my time when there's no way to reconnect and seemingly no way to preserve any of the progress you've already made.

review_text: V fun game with a few issues holding it back somewhat. I have little interest in pvp so this is a brief bullet point review of the campaign in coop. PROS: Absolutely stunning game with incredible detail especially in the environments Great sound effects, very satisfying headshots Lots of cool additions from previous gears games, you can slide, climb, jump, hide behind much smaller cover while lying down and fight from different angles you couldnt before. Controls are smooth, smoothest they have ever been. Larger arena style combat encounters allowing many ways to tackle a fight TONS of weapons everywhere so you are almost never stuck using a weapon you dont want to use New weapon/armor mod system is excellent and allows you to customise your loadouts to make the gameplay style more personal to you and your choice of play style. This is my favourite addition to the game. Its excellent. Some very cool cutscenes and story segments Pretty solid soundtrack Good length Really really......meaty. Just a very fun chaotic blast of a game. CONS: Crashes....so many crashes. On average I crashed every hour or so. V annoying Semi open world sections were a bit of a swing and a miss at least in coop, One player is tethered to the other so if one goes too far away from the other you get teleported to him. This happened many times and was annoying. Full freedom to explore for both players should be available. Mods for weapons are scattered all around the world, finding them is well worth it but leads to a lot of exploring and wandering around and it kills the pace of the game a lot at points. The world is beautiful but I feel this kind of exploration clashes with the typically pretty fast paced gears of war gameplay style. The collectables are all marked on the map too as you get close so it takes from the feeling of discovery and often feels like you are just ticking off boxes on a checklist. I personally think they should have stuck with a fully linear approach to gears but keep the large arena style fights. New characters are so so. Would have rather they focus more on just Dom and Marcus and make it their game really. Final Score 7.5/10

title: Planet Zoo 2
review_text: I don't normally leave reviews so early, but due to a lot of negative reviews, I think these have been somewhat unfair and could lead to a false narrative so I shall leave mine, to help balance the view and if you are considering the game, make an educated choice. First the good: The tools in this game are fantastic. The pathing is especially good, better than Planet Coaster 2. Once you get used to the GUI, you will appreciate the tools more and understand the depth that the game goes down too, it is quite deep in parts. Graphics are next level, the detail in the animals and the movement is far superior to anything else before it. Career mode is the usual tutorial type mode but essential this time, especially to understand the new reserves game play. Performance has been very good, for me, since day 1. Yes my spec is mediocre in these times, but it runs well. Not had any crashes to desktop at all in my 30+ hours so far. Frontier have been good so far, with 2 patches in the first week. This is not like Planet Coaster 2, which agreeable had a shoddier launch. There is quite a few animals, I think 150 or so, available at launch, but you have to go through an unlocking system in franchise, but in sandbox you can have access from the getgo Building habitats, structures and terrain manipulation is far easier in this game than ever before, Building and terrain are far easier here than even in Planet Coaster 2. Its fantastic how you can path up to and into habitats, and the fence line will cut it making it so easy to remove the pathing inside habitats whilst butting up the path right to the fence line. The negative: It took me a while to enjoy the look of zoo 2 - it utilises very washed out colours (pastel-like). It sounds a silly thing, but PLANCO2 pops out to you from the menu, whereas zoo 2 didn.t Franchise is hard. Its locked behind a progression system that is very challenging. Franchise point is you need multiple zoo's and reserves, which cost conservation credits (CC), the one currency you run out of real quick (you can buy with CC or in game cash). The progression system locks animals behind a wall until you progress a couple of zoo's to 3 star and one reserve to 3 star to get to tier 3 (there are 5 #levels) is a particular challenge. Tho I am enjoying it, Frontier have committed to patch this to make it easier. The blueprints from frontier (the way you see them) is clunky and feels slow. review_text: Torn on recommending this game or not. If you want to jump into the Sandbox and start building, it is honestly a really great game. New stuff and improvements from Planet Zoo 1. To even complete what is needed for the 3-5 star reserves, you need to breed and sell animals as a major focus of your gameplay in a broken player-based market where one shoal of Common Rudd goes for 1000 credits or more. Tell me: [h3] Why does a conservation-focused zoo game make speculative animal trading such an important part of progression, rather than rewarding cooperation between zoos, species recovery programs, and sustainable population management? [/h3] Selling critically endangered animals on a speculative animal market, so you can then afford to buy other critically endangered animals on a speculative animal market, so you can then mass breed those critically endangered animals to sell on the speculative animal market, so you can then afford to buy and breed animals to release some onto a reserve. All while educating your guests on how the illegal animal markets are making many animals critically endangered. All that...just so you can then finally build your zoo with animals you think are neat. Until Franchise mode, the extreme market inflation, and the reserve systems are tweaked and fixed, just buy the game and play in Sandbox mode. At least in Sandbox, you can build a zoo you want in a game that is supposed to be about building a zoo and conservation. I recommend the game for the most part, but just know what you're getting into by buying it now.

review_text: I think it's a meaningful upgrade from Planet Zoo, while offering less overwhelming and more user friendly tools. I really enjoy the addition of the Wildlife Reserves is really engaging and exciting. I do wish there were more wildlife reserve locations, as three in Europe feels a little excessive when there are none in North America. Franchise mode now has accreditation tiers which is an additional challenge if that's what you're looking for, but there's always Sandbox which now has more modes and customization for different gameplay styles. Paths are a little more user friendly, and the game itself is beautiful. The animal roster will undoubtedly grow with DLC as that's how these games are, and I look forward to the addition of more animals. It's worth noting Planet Zoo and Planet Coaster games are more involved than most other design focused games, they live in a tier all their own between a 3D modeling program and a true designer game. If you've ever 3D modeled on any level, you'll be at home in Planet Zoo as most building pieces snap together in a pleasing way. It is more involved than the Sims, or Zoo Tycoon 2 from a building perspective, but pre-made blueprints help to mimic the drag and drop building if that's what you want. Planet Zoo 2 adds uniform scaling which opens up possibility for building even more. I've only experienced a couple minor bugs and reported them so they can be fixed, but overall I'm very happy with the game. If you missed the pre-order bonus items, I would wait for a sale, but it's a fun game.

title: Fallout 76
review_text: Bethesda and ZeniMax Media: Two Sides of the Same Coin Stay away from this company if you value your dignity and time. They banned my ESO account, into which I invested thousands of hours and money, based on false cheating accusations. Their support tickets provide no meaningful answers or evidence. They refer only to messages I exchanged with another player, interpreting “want to farm money?” as a reference to cheating. That is their justification. I have never experienced such unprofessionalism despite having played many games. At this point, there is no forgiveness for either of you. I recently got into this game and discovered what I had gotten myself into: “ZeniMax Media Terms of Service.” I'm seriously frustrated, and it is already too late to request a refund. Honest Overall Review 1. Company and Trust This company is dishonest, deceitful, and unprofessional. I say this clearly and without exaggeration. Evidence and recent reports can be found across well-known platforms. 2. Bugs and Unresolved Issues Many bugs have existed for years without being fixed. Here are some examples. 2.1. Stationary Enemies and Possible Exploits After an hour, I noticed that mobs in many houses stood completely still, even after detecting or attacking them. This allows players to farm XP without any challenge. I first noticed this inside a house near the northern or northeastern entrance to Whitespring Resort. I exploited the possible bug by luring mobs towards the door, making them return inside with reduced HP from my shots. Feel free to ban me for that! 2.2. Completely Bugged Main Quest "Thicker Than Water" This quest lets you kill Frankie or save him. If you choose to kill him, Beckett never fires his weapon, preventing completion. I replayed it six or seven times, trying different approaches and spending around ten minutes per attempt. Beckett simply stared at Frankie, and nothing happened. YouTube videos showed both players who successfully completed this choice and others experiencing the same bug. Reports dating back years suggest it remains unresolved. Against my wishes, I eventually saved Frankie and completed the quest without problems. 2.3. “Disconnected from Server” After an Update After a recent update, I started receiving “disconnected from server” when entering a server. I don't know whether it is connected to my banned ESO account or simply another bug. Online reports suggest resolution can take weeks. Given this company's policies, I fear another unjustified ban, even across different games. We buy games only to risk being banned without justification or evidence. I submitted a ticket because the servers appeared online and functional. This was when I discovered that ZeniMax is the “mother” behind this entire mess. 3. Customer Support My trust in this company is 0%. Search for “Fallout 76 bugs” and filter recent results to find countless unresolved issues. I encountered several myself but managed to work around them without seriously affecting gameplay. Gameplay 1. Difficulty, Progression, and Farming This is an easy game. I reached level 60 and learned around 90% of its content, including builds, trading, mutations, farming, and events. Some may find it complex, but I found it simple once I learned how everything worked, one thing at a time. The farming system is poor, especially for plants. They respawn based on how many other items you collect, not simply with time. You may need to collect around 1,000 other items before the original ones respawn. This is strange, confusing, and ridiculous. The beginning can be confusing because the game explains things poorly, but after several hours, you learn practically everything. 2. Missions and Group Activities Group missions are limited, extremely repetitive, sometimes slow, and generally too easy. I haven't tried every game mode, but a quick search will show you what to expect. 3. Inventory Management and Incentives to Spend Money Limited inventory space seems designed to encourage purchases. You must carefully manage your inventory and keep only essential items, spending considerable time doing so. Gameplay: Combat, AI, and Menus Combat “V.A.T.S.” is essentially an auto-aim mechanic against enemies, making it excellent for players with ping issues. Official servers are another advantage, particularly for players with Strict NAT connections. However, daily maintenance can take several hours. Artificial Intelligence (AI) The enemy AI is average. I cannot call it terrible, but it certainly isn't good either. Menus and Interface The menus are peculiar and interesting, but the experience is terrible. They are disorganized, difficult to manage, and lack decent filters. Inventory and quick-menu management waste time on tasks that should be simple. The game feels almost prehistoric in this regard. Assigning an item to the quick menu, such as key 3, can take almost a minute because finding it is so cumbersome. The favorites system helps little; the experience remains prehistoric. In-Game Market I would give it 4/10. It works, but I would not give it 5/10. Positive Points 1. Pay-to-Win (P2W) and Paid Advantages I couldn't determine with 100% certainty whether the game is P2W, but I am almost certain it isn't. The game encourages subscriptions for inventory benefits and other advantages. I managed my inventory by prioritizing damage and defense over perks or cards that reduce item weight or increase capacity. These perks make inventory management easier but reduce combat efficiency, especially when playing solo, as I do. 2. Busy Servers and Finding Groups Easily The servers are populated, and finding groups is easy. However, there is no in-game text chat, which is a downside, although voice chat is available. 3. Progression and Boss Difficulty Certain bosses can challenge beginners, but a decent weapon, such as a Gatling Gun, and safe positioning make combat extremely easy. Even with an average or poor build, defeating them is possible. Enemies with no stars or one or two stars require a good weapon, even without mods. With mods, you can eventually take on three- and four-star bosses solo. I never experienced a genuine feeling of difficulty. Leaving this game is therefore the best option for me. 4. Environment and Scenery The environment is beautiful. The variety of biomes and changing weather make the game more interesting. 5. Community The players I encountered, solo or in public groups, generally provided a positive experience. When someone gives you an item, it is usually because they no longer need it or consider it junk. Later, you will also leave many items behind. At first, however, they seem valuable because you have little equipment or do not yet understand the importance of inventory management. The game has a more mature player base. I hope they eventually break free from this addiction and stop supporting a company that deserves nothing but complete rejection. Summary and Ratings Performance, Stability and Servers: 8/10 Fun: 6/10 AI and Gameplay (Combat): 5/10 Story: I did not pay enough attention to evaluate it. P2W?: 7/10 - It does not seem pay-to-win, but I am not 100% certain. Trust in Bethesda/ZeniMax: 1/10 Bugs: 7/10 - Many remain unresolved for years. My worst experience was a main quest offering two choices, one of which did not work, forcing me to restart and choose the only option that allowed completion. Customer Support (Overall): 1/10 Overall Rating: 2/10 I thank the people responsible for this game for showing me “disconnected from server.” Without it, I might still have been tempted to spend money on a company that does not deserve my respect.

review_text: Okay so I downloaded this game on August 1st for ONE reason: Jingran. Saw him once and decided I'm installing a whole gacha game for him. Zero regrets. He's my main, he's getting his full resonance chain on his rerun, and I'm so glad I finally got the game. What I didn't expect was to fall this hard for everything else. The story is genuinely GOOD. I'm the person who refuses to skip dialogue, and this game rewards that. Mengzhou's arc had me emotionally invested in ways I was not prepared for, and the cutscenes are gorgeous. The music too is so well done. Combat feels SO good once it clicks. Swapping characters, Outro/Intro combos, landing a clean rotation, it's satisfying in a way that makes you want to keep building your team. The echo system is a whole rabbit hole too. Is it RNG pain sometimes? Absolutely, I once had seven bad rolls in a row. But when you finally hit that perfect substat on your last try? Best feeling in the world. The gacha is fair as these things go. You can lose 50/50s (ask me how I know), but the weapon banner is a guaranteed featured 5-star at pity, there's no 50/50 for weapons, and the game is generous enough that you can save up and actually plan your pulls. but.... a 50/50 pity system like the one in Genshin called Capturing Radiance would be so nice... because I have lost 4 50/50s and have yet to win one in this game. Exploration is fun,(I spend lots of time just looking for chests and minigames) the world is beautiful, and the characters are designed with so much love. Even the ones I'm not pulling for, I'm still invested in. 10/10, came for Jingran, stayed for literally everything else. Play it.

title: Aniimo
review_text: Want to understand the game? They use a HoYoverse template. What is that, Genshin Impact (I think) pioneered it but there is also Honkai Star Rail and Zenless Zone Zero with the same UI or Menu structures, upgrade loop, but with different themes, speaking of themes Aniimo is like Pal World meets the cozy HoYoverse originator, aka, Little Nikki. My take on Aniimo: I play it. I enjoy the story part. I have wasted some money on the passes and once on a reup to buy the music player for the farm (it was $5 one time payment) -- do you have to spend money, hell no. I completed the entire story without worrying about the farm or this or that, the end game between seasons is where they get you, casual players should have no problems, but the grind is capped (weekly limits on luckies, and other stuff to slow your collection roll), beyond that, the whole playing with someone else is so hobbled because they do not want people starting an aniimo trading economy (so becoming friends where you can trade your aniimo is painstakingly slow -- about a month or more, unless you pay to speed it up, or really focus on it, then you might do it in two weeks without money added). The bare truth (and the worst part of the game is the HoYoverse template): When you strip away the surface-level paint—whether it's cute creatures in Aniimo or fashion and floating platforms in Infinity Nikki—you realize you're looking at the exact same industrial assembly-line product. Pawprint use the same psychological hooks, the same map-clearing busywork, the same structural pacing, and often the exact same lazy narrative crutches (like a generic "Umbral" corruption force) just to give you a reason to open chests and grind materials. And I am okay with that for the most part, just know what you are getting, and be a WISE CONSUMER, because unless you are a Whale, you are just Chum. Long live the ANIIMO CHUM. So basically, PawPrint is NOT building a unique creative vision from the ground up; they are taking a pre-approved, highly profitable corporate blueprint and swapping out the assets. One team plugs in dresses and styling minigames, another plugs in creature-catching and an RV base, but the underlying machine ticking away underneath is identical. Once you see past the marketing veneer and spot the template, you can't unsee it. It makes you look at a game like Aniimo and realize that its biggest flaws—the lack of genuine soul, the repetitive filler content, the predictable story beats—aren't just isolated mistakes; they are baked right into the template it copied. And YET I find it Fun regardless of this Truth. So that is why I recommend it, if you can go in with eyes wide open, then its all good. Manage Expectations, those surveys probably will not change the core of the game, but then again MONEY TALKS SO MAYBE (its like a .005% chance of rolling) THEY REALLY SAVE THIS FROM THE DIRECTION OF METOCRITY AND CASH GRABBY DESCIONS THAT MAKE THE TIME BETWEEN THE STORY AND NEW ANIIMO FEEL LIKE BEING A JUNKY SEARCHING FOR CRACK SCRAPS IN THE CARPET. PS some RV/Farming events/products (which are co-op) are only for The Red Book Players on Chinese Servers, region blocked, beyond the GREAT RED FIRE WALL (but you can see over a little because, the co-op farmable is show in all regions, international tease). review_text: Alright so i'll cut up this review into 3 little parts: Content, progression and performance. I have 127 hours at the time of this review and will keep it as clean as possible. Ignoring the outside noise and focusing on the game. Pt; 1 Content. (3 major things to do, egg heist, homeland and normal world exploration) At first i was quite pleased, it's a pretty world with honestly good music and atmosphere in most areas. Most Aniimo look part of a living breathing world. Sadly outside of a few areas there are exactly 0 NPC's who just want to battle with you so there's no real story outside the sea of flowers. As for things to do, most things are heavily monetized to prevent you from accomplishing anything other than catch the aniimo 1000 times or play egg heist until your eyes come out because there's not much else to do once you've done your daily nutures to get a chance to sniff a prismana aniimo. Homeland is a niche addition that requires little attention since most things are automatic but in general it's ok. Yes you can tell there's definitive AI in some aspects of the game like the music and translation since some things are ROUGH. 2. Progression, I'd rather cheese grate the bottom of my feet than have to go through the progression of this game again. At first super hand holdy, then it throws you off boat never to be seen again. Once you use the early game stuff you're essentially S.O.L. until the next patch rolls around unless you're a nepo baby. Monetization litterally runs all late game progression to the near point of snufffing out all progress at all. (hitting egg emperor with 49 days left in the cycle would essentially force you to play the hardest difficulty for 9 hours every single day until the end of the cycle and there's nothing to bypass this.) Needless to say progression is by far the worst thing in this game. Performance and Looks; For what this game is and for how half baked it is, it's not terrible, though the Dev disconnect certainly will not help it. It looks good and perfoms mostly consistenly well on a I9, 32GB quad core, 4090. Some performance issues in long sessions (4+ hrs) but rather smooth. Looks as i said before are generally very good and the landscapes are really nice in most areas. The aniimo have something for everyone there's good variety and playstyles but limited roles. If you skipped over everything that i just wrote and come straight to the bottom for a two line resume: The game was pulled out of the oven too early, monetization strangles progress, and you have to be jobless (in terms of time) to get most rewards before the cycles shift. I wouldn't spend money on this game unless you adore it and plan to make it a long term investment. Oh yeah and the in game support is practically non existent.

title: MapleStory
review_text: I'm reviewing Classic I've played Maplestory as my main mmorpg, off and on since Ludibrium was first added. Over the years I've wanted something like a classic version of this game that isn't a private server, and finally we have one. First impressions are that it looks and feels like Maplestory as it was pre-Big Bang. It was refreshing. The leveling curve was as grindy as I remembered, and all the old places and spots were as they were. The game was stripped of most of the bloat that the main game currently has. I did notice some changes that I didn't expect like new skills, new level requirements, and new ways to fuel the in-game economy that wasn't introduced in the game back then. Most of my experience has been positive, however my current issues with the game are the current limitations. Maple has never made it easy to boost ones in-game financial stability in the early days, and this part of the game has revealed itself again. You are almost dedicated to the market as much as you are to grinding and leveling up. Not to mention that the current state of the in-game economy (and RL tbf) is unstable and fluctuating daily, and it feels like spending is thin among the general population yet there's shops everywhere, and not enough shop space in the Free Market on ALL channels. Again, you would have to commit to the market and use up a lot of time that could be used elsewhere. Also, the need to fill ones own pocket almost requires you spend money in order to do so. TLDR: The game is great if you are going in for nostalgia or to experience the greatness of the early days of Maplestory, but it is tough for anyone new and unwilling to spend actual money. I am hopeful since I am only playing the founders early access version, that the game will open up when F2P arrives, and that more will be added to stabilize the game.

title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse
review_text: I have played Castlevania games since the Sega Genesis and have been waiting a looong time for a new entry. I played the game in one 24 hour long marathon and have a bunch of thoughts on it that I will break down. First how it looks. Simply amazing, holding the gothic/romantic horror style I love so dearly. Everything and everyone looks amazing, I just love Rose's character design. Weapons are just so cool to look at when using them, EXSPECALLY the whips. Paris and Dracula's Castle was beautiful to behold. Hard to say what was my fav. Notre Dame, that would be the closest. The story. I was a bit nervous about this, when I watched the inde showcase earlier this year I was left with a feeling that the team did not know much about the lore and left alot of fans speculating on what timeline they were going to follow. Turns out they know quite a bit and decided to fallow the game cannon and faithfully to the tic. Rose fits nicely in the cannon and all the references to other characters including Adrian ( Of course ) and Hector was very nice to see. Achievements. Thankfully all the games cheevos are within a common gamers grasp with exception to finishing the game in four hours ( I personally just hate speed-running things. ) Music and sound in general. Ok this is my first negative. My father and Castlevania shaped my taste in music and in Belmont's Curse it's..ok. Most of it is kind of repetitive, nothing that will get you head bopping and ingrained into memory. It all kinda blends together with only a little difference depending on area. I am quite sad about this as I saw a teaser trailer that sounded like they were going to do a mix of " A Toccata into blood soaked Darkness" from Cod, a personal fav of mine. But it never showed. Nothing about the soundtrack makes me want to find rips of it to add my my car mp3 or listen to a 10 hour extension of a singular track. I found this kinda baffling as the team behind this made a whole cover list for there game Dead Cells for the Castlevania crossover and it was awesome. For general sound, its great, all crispy and punchy, The gameplay, In general. This is through and through MetroidVania at its best. It's everything I love about the genera. Combat is sold and the game is on the longer side, took me about 18 hours of ingame time to fully 100% it all. Though points are lost on not telling you how to use the mirror save room as transport , I only found that out by looking it up online while trying to save the woman in the mirror. The fewer selection of weapons was at first a sad choice but I quickly dropped the sadness on finding that each weapon class has its own combat mechanics, personal fav is whips, though Fists come close. They all feel good to use, sold, flashy, fun, and unique. The tarot cards are a nice callback to circle of the moons Card DDS system, not the same but they act like different spells that all have varying affects. Some way more busted than other. All cards have little mini-quests too that power them up. Monsters all have their own movesets, all of them. It's cool and with the ability to perfect block freaking everything I am sure a crazy person will one day do a no hit run of this. Though speaking of the blocking system I should get on to my mixed feeling part of the gameplay. Difficulty. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hell. Without modification ( We will get to that in a sec. ) This game can be frustratingly difficult. Many times during the early game I was starting to get agitated with all the little things that was just grinding my mind down like axe armors throwing a axe after dieing, or mermen AA gunning your ass outa the sky. It is forgiving in some aspects, like if you die after unlocking something it wont roll back if you die and getting back is mostly pain free...if you know about teleport via mirror. ( CROUCH AT THE MIRRORS FOR LIKE 6 SECONDS.). But yea some monsters are rough. I struggled on some bosses like Medusa and ranged mobs WERE MY BAIN, I sucked so hard with the perfect blocking. Things changed like halfway through the game though, I just started spamming the perfect block and found that doing so I can block like 50% of bosses attacks, with leveling and the waaay busted King Arthur tarot card I tanked and one shot the last four bosses including Dracula twice ( Two endings, well three but two at that moment. ). I started having ALOTA fun during the late game on the bog standard setting, about that. The difficulty setting is not yer regular easy, med, and hard but a selection of sliders. You can change damn near everything -WITHOUT PENILTY- the damage mobs/bosses do from one hit to freaking nothing, toggle DEATH, add or subtract healing pots ( Lota souls vibe's added Pots are like the Souls OJ.), toggle how much damage you do from a whimper to GOD INCARNATE, and a few others including a toggle to spawn you at the boss room door and not the save room ( Out of all of them I recommend this be turned on.). This is the best thing I ever seen when It comes to setting how hard you want the game to be and I seriously recommend customizing the game to fit how hard/easy you like to play the game and not just tough it out like a moron, aka, me. Overall this is the Castlevania I was waiting for, I am happy things turned out so well overall. Thanks for this <3. On a side note for game performance, I added my rig specs to the review. I had no issues whatsoever. BUT for ultra-wide monitor peeps, it can go Ultrawide by hitting Ctrl-Enter a few times but It breaks the UI. PLEASE add proper support for this.

title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse
review_text: I'll get this out of the way now: Castlevania Belmont's Curse is not perfect and doesn't surpass the likes of Symphony of the Night or Aria of Sorrow, but I really enjoyed it regardless. I'll admit that I was a little wary when I saw that the game had a flask system and enemies respawned with every use of the save room. I have a bit of "Hollow Knight Fatigue" but thankfully this game manages to avoid the "blue-balling" a lot of Modern MetroidVania games like to do by adequately rewarding conquering challenging platforming and combat with new weapons and badges frequently. That being said, I kept reading the negative reviews and videos up through release and during my playthrough and... I'm sorry but were we even playing the same game? The level of absolutely moronic takes I've seen about this game is astounding. Stuff ranging from: "mobile game quality," to having bad art, to saying that Rose is like the other annoying girlbosses that have plagued modern gaming, and I don't see it. People are complaining that it's not exactly like the IgaVania games, and while it's fine to prefer those games, that doesn't make this game bad in any shape or form. If you want to play nothing but Iga's games, and you're not open to trying anything different, then play Ritual of the Night and Scarlet Inquisition when it releases. If you don't like the different musical style this game goes for, then that's also fair, but I've seen idiots complain that this game is "Dead Cells 2" and also complain that it doesn't play enough like Dead Cells, or that it's not a Roguelike despite the fact that nowhere in this game's marketing did it ever even imply that it was going to be a Roguelike. I quite like the added emphasis on platforming this game brings back from Classic Castlevania on top of the MetroidVania structure from Symphony and onwards. I really enjoy the greater emphasis on puzzle solving and environmental clues to progress through the game, which reminded me a lot of Symphony of the Night in particular, but also the Metroid Prime series. And even the music grew on me despite it not being like anything we've seen in Castlevania before. Also if you're a Castlevania lore fan like I am, this game is an absolute love letter to fans who are very familiar with the continuity of the series. Fans of the PS2 Castlevania Duology will see that those games are especially given lots of love and attention by this game. I've seen people complain that a Castlevania game, the franchise that's the namesake of the "Vania" half of MetroidVania, isn't reinventing the wheel with their first mainline 2D game in almost 20 years. Frankly, I don't think a series that invented half of that original wheel is obligated to reinvent it, and Belmont's Curse competently modernized Castlevania anyways. Now with all that out of the way, here are my actual, legitimate nitpicks with this game: 1. The light whip grapple likes to get confused on which target I intend to grapple to, especially when an enemy and a grapple point are within close proximity of one another. 2. Whether I executed the light whip grapple attack or not wasn't as consistent as I really thought it ought to be. There were times it felt like I just had to tap the attack button while grappling towards an enemy, and sometimes I had to deliberately hold the button down. 3. The parry is just weird and I'm not the biggest fan of its wonky hitbox. I'm a Royal Guard main in DMC and I absolutely love perfect parrying attacks any chance I get, but it seems like there are times where parrying works how I'd expect it to in other games (pressing the button right as an attack collides with Rose) and sometimes it wants me to parry far in advance. Like the attack has to hit the edge of the bubble surrounding Rose for it to count, and it doesn't feel consistent no matter how hard I tried to get it down. When I got to the end of my 100% Item Completion playthrough, I felt like I could parry certain attacks consistently, but other attacks not at all. 4. The devs of this game either need to add checkpoints to the outside of boss doors or move Save Points closer to the Boss Rooms like in every other non-linear Castlevania game. It's really annoying to die to a boss (which you will do a lot in this game because it's hard) and then spend 5-10 minutes jogging back to the Boss Room to try again from the newrest Save Room. Most of the time there are no enemies or meaningful obstacles in the way so what's the point? You don't even lose map progress, resources, or collected items if you die before saving again so it's just unnecessary padding between attempts to learn an already difficult boss's patterns. Anyways, this game might as well be a masterpiece for MetroidVania fans considering it's only $30 full price and I hope this game does well so that we can potentially get that Demon Castle War of 1999 game at long last.

title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse
review_text: 100%ed the game and it was absolutely worth it to me as a Castlevania fan, especially for the price! Exploration is fun and rewarding, new weapons or relics you find all at least feel like they have a use case and I found myself experimenting a lot more than I usually do with the builds I go for. The abilities you unlock, while not ground-breaking, are incredibly fun and while I won't spoil later stuff the whip grapple you get early on is so sick. Really feels fluid especially in combat. Backtracking isn't nearly as much of an issue as other titles in this genre are, with an abundance of fast travel opportunities as you progress and a fairly tight map layout along with each room turning gold in the map overlay so you know when you're done with an area. Yes it's still here but it doesn't feel nearly as much of a chore like other games like it. Combat is fun and the weapon/arcana variety makes me naturally experiment more. There's not too much enemy variety but given the game isn't too long I didn't really feel it and the abundance of bosses makes up for it! While I wasn't the biggest fan of the music at first (as someone who prefers the punchier tracks to more atmospheric background noise) it really grew on me and it helped make each area and encounter feel unique and exciting. There's some fantastic tracks and renditions in here that I won't spoil but going in with an open mind really goes a long way. I'm a huge fan of the art style too! This game is gorgeous and you can screenshot at basically any point and it's eye candy, with some superb designs or set pieces and the lighting especially it really can't be understated how clean it all looks. Something I always appreciate about good action platformers/Metroidvanias is the opportunity to try your own thing, maybe it's not always intended but some small skips or tricks you can do to access stuff early (grappling onto flying enemies for height or just good hitbox manoeuvring what helps keep this genre fresh especially on replays and feels awesome to pull off. This "trying your own thing" also extends to your playstyles in combat where you can either relax and spam the strong arcanas/weapons or go for something more engaging and challenge yourself with weaker items and the gameplay settings to make the game easier/harder really plays well into that mindset. I think a lot of people judge a game based off how easy/hard the path of least resistance is but it's a singleplayer game, I promise nobody's stopping you from playing how you want. Story-wise it was really satisfying too, as someone who's a huge fan of Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse and someone who's played and Curse of Darkness, as well as other titles I won't get into for the sake of avoiding spoilers it felt like a natural fit into the world, celebrating the past while still leaving its own mark. The voice acting is fantastic too, having Graham McTavish back alone is great. I'm also grateful 100%ing hasn't taken me too long, I'm not a fan of insanely long 100% requirements so this felt substantial enough without overstaying its welcome and I can only think of it fondly and it's a shame to see the discourse surrounding it be so reductive and refuse to articulate genuine issues beyond social media gotcha posts. I don't really have any proper flaws on my mind with this game. I don't expect it to become #1 by any means but I can't think of anything that truly impacted my playthrough! Very pleasant from beginning to end and I have to commend the developers for the final result. Also the key art is god tier.

title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse
review_text: Good Castlevania. Not an Igavania successor. Let’s start with the good stuff: the gameplay is FUN. Combat feels smooth and responsive, the handmade art looks gorgeous, and the character designs are insanely cool. Just running around, fighting enemies and killing bosses feels great. BUT... The castle is way too small. Especially if you grew up with Symphony of the Night, you’ll probably finish exploring it thinking, “Wait... that’s it?” Enemy variety is also pretty weak. You fight the same monsters repeatedly, and worse, their drops aren’t interesting enough to make grinding satisfying. In Igavania games, I could spend an embarrassing amount of time killing the same enemy just to get some stupidly rare sword, armor, spell, or item. Here? Not really. And the music is good but...yeah. Very forgettable. That hurts because Castlevania music is supposed to be HALF THE EXPERIENCE. SOTN and the classic Igavanias had tracks I still remember years later. Here, I finished playing and could barely remember any of them. VERDICT: 8/10 This is a very fun, beautiful, and genuinely cool Castlevania game. I absolutely enjoyed my time with it and would recommend it. But a spiritual successor to Igavania? Nope. That title still belongs to Bloodstained Series. Recommended - just don’t go in expecting another Symphony of the Night.

review_text: As a long-time fan of 2D Castlevania games, I was pleasantly surprised—even though the game felt more like Metroid than Castlevania. The game is an entertaining and appropriately challenging experience. Visually, the game is pleasing, with a clear focus on detail. The areas are expansive and packed with details; it’s easy to overlook items or clues when your attention is focused elsewhere. The soundtrack, however, could have used more effort. No track really stood out or stuck in my memory—not even the version of "Bloody Tears." Overall, the music felt too generic; it wasn't quite "elevator music," but it wasn't far off, either. One aspect of the gameplay that could have used a bit more thought is the "Mirrors of Life" fast-travel system. It’s clunky and requires a lot of effort to get from one place to another. I’d give it a solid 7 out of 10. *** SPOILER *** The game features three different endings; I played through all of them, which took 20 hours on my first playthrough (99.6% completion).

title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse
review_text: I give this about a 7.5/10. It's not a top tier Castlevania, but it's solid. It does a few things differently, and that's rubbed a very vocal minority of screeching twits the wrong way into saying it's "not Castlevania". It absolutely is, but this is going to come off as a harsh review for a thumbs up here. Harsh because of what keeps it from greatness. First, the music. At first, I liked the chill synth grooves, but then I realised that practically all of the music is like this. There's not a lot of variety. Sure, there's a number of different, unique, tracks, but they're all kind of samey. There's no baroque metal, here. It's not "bad" music, it just doesn't have the vibe I've come to expect. Second, the platforming. To be clear, I do enjoy it. It's not standard Castlevania fare. Dashes, walljumps and double-jumps chained with whip swings. It has more in common with Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown than with previous Castlevanias. That's not a bad thing, but The Lost Crown executes the concept far better, both in terms of being more challenging, and in terms of reserving the most challenging stuff for purely and obviously optional content. The baseline difficulty in TLC is higher, the ceiling is MUCH higher, but the essential path stuff in Belmont's Curse is harder than the surrounding game would prepare you for. Third, weapons. The game has several major weapon types, and four weapons in each type. The weapons are straight tier improvements, with no reason to use a weapon from an earlier tier, ever, if you have the later one. Compare this to Aria of Sorrow, where you have numerous weapons in each class, each with their own damage arcs, and potential elemental effects. It's less deep than previous Castlevania games. The weapon types all feel decent, but there's nothing to differentiate them strongly until you get their Legendary tier weapons, which each have unique effects. Fourth, the Relics. You can equip three at once. I haven't seen if there's a way to increase that. There's never a reason to have fewer than three equipped. The effects are all kind of bland, like these were thrown in because the kind of combat this game has seems to require them, but there wasn't a lot of thought into how they change up the balance. It's another thing Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown executes significantly better. It's not bad, but it's not fleshed out well. Fifth, this brings us to the combat. There isn't a useless spell in the game, and all of your traversal upgrades apply in combat, too, so big thumbs up, there. No traversal upgrade stops at just being a key to a door. This is rarer than you'd think, in metroidvanias. The negative here is, the combat is just not that deep. You have your directional attacks, and your whip grapples, and not much else. The slide is introduced kind of like it should behave as a dodge roll and it does not. It's just a positioning tool. That's fine, but I think the pace of the combat sets the expectation of a dodge roll. There's also just less technical depth to this. Again, I compare it to PoP: TLC. TLC crams in basically a whole 2D fighter's worth of mechanical depth, with a lot of variety in just how your hits can land. You have launchers and pokes, moves for zoning, moves for closing distance fast. You even start to get a feel for frame advantage and "turns" in TLC's BASIC combat. You just don't have that depth in Belmont's Curse. Where Curse comes out ahead compared to TLC is it doesn't flag parryable and dodge-requiring attacks with big glowing indicators. Figure it out. It's let down by the parry feeling very much like a "the game should have one" afterthought, doubling up on the Holy Light ability's use, but without much in the way of dedicated combat mechanics that make use of it. You can easily forget you even have a parry. As for the good, map design is strong. Distance between save rooms can be a bit much, at times, but the path between save rooms actually seems to emulate the style of classic Castlevania games. It's like the paths have been thought out as stages, which is neat. Different zones of the map often have different mechanics or gimmicks making them feel unique. The two fast travel systems (one of them semi-hidden) are a bit insufficient in the early game, and unlocking the full power of the hidden system is a very late-game thing, done incidentally to another optional goal, but it is an absolute SLOG to do it. I think that second fast travel system should have just been accessible from the start (it IS, but in a form limited to your current zone), and drop the Ferryman entirely. The story, it draws heavily on Lament of Innocence. There aren't many surprises here, it's a bit paint by numbers, but the story does its job. It's got a minimalist frame that can give you early justification for filling out your tarot deck just as a matter of course, and the tarot deck does integrate into finding your way to, and getting hints on, each boss. As the Metroidvania half of Castlevania goes, I put this in my list somewhere above Circle of the moon. What it does differently to what is standard for Castlevania is welcome, but suffers for not committing to it fully. Everything it does differently, strangely enough, is executed better by The Lost Crown. It's overall an easier, less good Lost Crown with a gothic vampire skin on it. I enjoyed The Lost Crown, it's actually my favourite Metroidvania, so this similarity is not a bad thing, to me. I just judge Curse harshly for failing to commit fully to the ideas it borrows.

title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse
review_text: A great revival for the series, but the boss fights let me down a bit ​It's a masterpiece. The locations, boss designs, and overall atmosphere are simply top-tier. ​Exploring the world for secrets and lore is genuinely interesting. The mirror system, arcanas, and weapon implementation are a definite plus, and the UI and progression system are very convenient and intuitive. You can immediately tell the developers approached the legendary franchise with massive respect, adding a ton of details that true Castlevania fans will definitely appreciate. ​The platforming was a pleasant surprise for me. I didn't expect such intense and precise parkour in Castlevania where you have to use your abilities with absolute finesse, as it's not very typical for classic Igavanias, but it turned out to be a really cool evolution. When you fall for the 10th time but finally make that jump to get the loot it's an incredible feeling. ​But there is one "but": the boss fights. I expected a much bigger challenge, especially from the final boss, but unfortunately, this aspect let me down. You can basically just spam attack almost all of them. And yes, there is a difficulty slider in the settings that allows you to make enemies more lethal. But simply changing damage numbers doesn't make their AI any smarter or trickier. ​Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the story and my journey to completion. It would be great to see post-game modes added later, which is typical for the series. And also, please finally add some items to the Token Shop!

title: RuneScape: Dragonwilds
review_text: Wasn’t sure I’d enjoy it, but I was very wrong! As a long-time OSRS player, I was initially quite unsure about Dragonwilds. I’ve never really been interested in survival games or base building, so I wasn’t convinced this would be for me. Well, I bought it, jumped in with a friend, and ended up playing for four hours on our first night. Safe to say, I absolutely loved it! The game manages to capture a lot of that familiar RuneScape feeling while offering something completely different. The skilling and progression feel rewarding, and even the base building, which I thought I’d dislike, has actually been enjoyable. One thing I’d definitely recommend is playing with a friend. There’s naturally a fair bit of grinding involved, but it’s RuneScape, so that’s hardly a surprise! Progression starts off fairly quick and gradually slows down, exactly as you’d expect. I don’t mind that at all, but having someone alongside you makes gathering resources, levelling skills and exploring much more enjoyable. It really helps break up the grind. The random dragon attacks are another brilliant touch. They keep you on your toes and make the world feel dangerous and unpredictable. Just when you’re getting comfortable doing your own thing, a dragon turns up to remind you that you’re not entirely safe! A few things I’d love to see added in future updates: * Dragon Dagger (DDS) – One of my favourite OSRS weapons. I’d love to see its iconic double-hit special attack and poison damage make their way into Dragonwilds. * Dragon Longsword – Another classic, ideally with its Cleave special attack. * More Scimitars – It’s great seeing familiar weapons like the Rune and Dragon Scimitars, but I’d love the full classic range eventually. I really like the existing special attack system, and I think bringing more of those iconic OSRS weapon abilities into Dragonwilds would be fantastic. Overall, I’m genuinely impressed. I went in expecting that I might not enjoy it, and instead found myself not wanting to log off. If you’re an OSRS player who’s on the fence like I was, I’d definitely recommend giving it a go, especially if you can convince a friend to join you. Really looking forward to seeing how the game develops. Keep up the good work, Jagex!
