title: RuneScape: Dragonwilds
review_text: Would I recommend this game? Hell No. This has the outward appearance of being a fine-but-generic open world, survival-ish RPG. Unfortunately, it in no way reaches the bare minimum of even an average game. It is littered with bugs and balancing issues at every turn, appearing to be coded by an AI with sheer absurdity of the number (and severity) of bugs that will appear in the space of an hour. Many of which have already appeared in patches DURING my playthrough stated to have been fixed that have not only NOT gotten fixed, but have been made worse, accompanied by the addition of yet MORE bugs from the very patch that was supposed to have had the fix. [b]Worldgen:[/b] The game world can be easily summed up with one word: Ugly. Aside from the small starting area that's a nice green forested area, intended to be built in for new players. The rest of the significantly larger map is a disgusting mix of mismatching colors and textures. Larger areas like Fellhollow are so ugly (both visibly and audibly) that in no way would you consider building there, yet make up a significant portion of the world. Leaving only the Fractured Plains as a potential place to live, if one likes red plants and purple trees where your house will stand out in a bad way. The rest of the map is populated with enemies, but little in the way of interesting details or landmarks. [b]Combat:[/b] Combat is bad at every stage of the game. Everything uses stamina, but blocking, dodging and attacking use significantly more stamina than is reasonable. While there are things to reduces stamina usage, it comes at a far worse cost elsewhere for too little of a trade-off. Even if dodging used less stamina, it only really works in some circumstances as player and enemy hitboxes and colliders regularly interfere with each other when moving causing you to be trapped under/inside an enemy and unable to move/evade/escape (Again, buggy game). Meanwhile, blocking is simply not effective: One can perfect block/parry with precise timing but the window is too small and many enemies perform erratic behaviour before actually landing their attacks and they will regularly use heavy attacks designed to break your block, making a build dependent on blocking largely useless. It also doesn't help that melee builds are heavily penalized against any sort of boss. Almost all fights, especially lategame are won through cheesing, by climbing onto a tall object and firing a dozen arrows/bolts/spells onto the non-ranged enemies. It's not fun, it's not skillful; it's a tactic of first and last resort when dealing with broken combat mechanics and overly-zealous hitboxes. [b]Survival:[/b] Like any survival-ish games: You need food, water, rest. Farming provides more of any resource than you'll ever need, but you'll farm for the sake of farming simply because the food in the game is terribly balanced. Food provides both sustenance (hunger) and health. This is the ONLY way to recover health immediately, and is penalized by causing the Over Eating status effect. There are no potions and no healing items, even though certain crafting materials say they're used in recovery potions, it's a lie. In fact, food is so badly balanced that some foods restore more hunger than your bar can hold, causing Over Eating immediately. Many expensive and complicated foods provide no buffs, making their entire existence unnecessary. Drinks available allow you to have ONE drink buff, just as food gives you ONE food buff; these typically reduce the stamina cost of spells, melee attacks, ranged attacks, dodging, OR give regeneration. Because only one can be used, you're probably going to go with regeneration for most fights. [b]Building:[/b] A surprising highlight of the game: The building system is decent. It's not amazing, but leveling the Construction skill to unlock new building parts is... terrible. You would need to build a monumental mansion with the basic starting wood blocks in order to unlock the next "Cottage" building set, which is itself unnecessarily expensive to build. (WHY does this need not one, but TWO stone types ground into powders for walls?! It should be Clay and Oak, it should not require iron-tier progression!!) It's too much work for too little gain. There is no replace function when building; so there's no way to replace existing walls, floors and foundations with newer, nicer-looking ones at a later time. You've gotta tear the whole thing down. Base Attacks occur fairly regularly, but their difficulty is based on where your base is located. As such, if you're to build where it tells you, in the Bramblemead Valley, you will suffer repeated losses at the hands of waves of goblin warriors and archers before you're equipped to even fight them. This is because you won't have Level 2 weapons and armor until later. Especially if you're stopping to build a base to live in, and most encounters with enemies in the wild will be 1v1 and in a base attack you'll be fighting 5v1. Again, combat bad. Not enough stamina. You'll be fighting 3 melee dudes in armor and 2 ranged archers. This problem gets significantly worse if you build in the Fractured Plains (no one is building in either swamp or the highlands). There are no defenses or traps to defend your base. They will break your walls down to get to you. [b]Spells and Resources:[/b] Mining sucks. It would be a punishment if not for the Rocksplosion spell. Ore nodes that generate on cave walls and ceilings, when broken will usually spit their ores through the wall/ceiling and out of bounds, falling into the void unless you're determined to slam your head into the ceiling in the hopes of sucking them up from outside the world. The colliders on ore nodes are larger than the model, causing a player who climbs/walks over a node to mine it float in the air and preventing you from mining ores that should otherwise be in reach. Trees when cut down, always seem to fall in the opposite direction that you want them to, making the ability to maximize the use of the Splinter spell impossible. Moreso since you can't push or roll trees together. Not good. Spectral Arrows is the only spell for bows and it's useless. Enemies don't line up for penetration to ever be useful. It provides no damage bonus, no ammo use reduction, no bonus vs undead, nothing. Fire Spirit (Runecrafting) unlocks WAY too late to be useful. It should be available as one of the first spells unlocked as it replaces the otherwise useless torch. This has already gone on long enough. So i'm gonna add a few more gripes: Most armors are ugly. You will not wear a full armor set because their full set effects are bad. Combat is bad. You will regularly rubberband back into enemies because you tried to roll out of an attack and because the enemy's arm happened to occupied that space 20 seconds ago, will treat it like a wall and you'll go nowhere. You can't fight any boss with a melee weapon because they all have high-damage, high-speed melee attacks that are so big you can't dodge or block. If you push the attack/mine/chop/dodge button once, you'll perform the action 2-3 times, wasting time, stamina and durability. Bows will regularly bug out and be unable to be fired. The fix is to double-jump. Yes, that is a regular bug that will occur several times an hour and YES that is the fix. Hence, why this game must surely be AI-coded. If you enter a vault, you will lose your ability to change weapons, open inventory, open the menu, everything. The fix is to Alt+F4. This is one of those bugs that was supposed to be fixed, but obviously isn't. You will at the worst times imaginable, fall through the ground into the void; roll or jump in a direction you were NOT facing or moving (and is usually when you're somewhere high up). And... i'm done. Tl;dr Game is bad. Full of bugs. Full of bad balance. Full of bad decisions.

review_text: It's digital MtG, so if you like to play the game but don't want to haul or sort your collection this is for you. Let's talk monetization, because that is the worst part of any game like this. But the thing is, free-to-play in this game DOES NOT mean pay-to-win. You can spend stupid amounts of money on your collection if that's your thing, but you really don't need to spend a dime. Season passes? Yes, those are here, but you can actually earn the gems to unlock them through free play. You earn gold through daily quests (easily earned through starter deck duels, so you're never at a wealth disadvantage) and then you can spend that gold to enter draft competitions to win gems. The conversion rates will depend on your win rate, but you can absolutely EARN the premium currency rather than paying real money. There are more play modes than I can even count with events and opportunities constantly shifting. Some of them (constructed and historic, mainly) will be full of players with the strongest decks that money can buy, and anyone who hasn't made that kind of investment is going to lose a LOT. Still, even on your first day you'll likely have enough wildcards to build *one* such deck--but after that you'll need to pay for more wildcards or earn them very slowly before you'll have enough to build another.

title: Star Trek: Outposts Unknown
review_text: I will admit, I was a bit surprised when someone said they were making a Star Trek city-builder game, I daresay even skeptical. I tried the Alpha-demo that was briefly available back in the summer (June-July 2026) and I was hooked, with many hours playing in its unfinished state and now also the post-launch (~100hrs total). [h1]...The Quick and Dirty[/h1] [h2]Overall Score: 7.5 out of 10[/h2] [code] X - Would Purchase at $70+ ✔ - Would Purchase at $30 X - Would rather wait for large Steam discount [/code] [h1]... The not-so-quick and dirty[/h1] [h2]Ratings Breakdown:[/h2] [b]Art/Look: 7/10[/b] These are clearly human-created assets. Drawn maps/terrain for each planet. Custom designed character models (according to the devs, most character models were pretty much copy/paste from the IRL Dev team (with a few 'alien' features added for the non-humans) ) The building design is fairly cohesive for most of the structures - you can tell they're all from the same group. The only problem might be that they don't necessarily "feel" like Star Trek - but this presents it's own issue since we don't really know what 'Star Trek' buildings look like, aside from the super fancy/curved edifices of Starfleet Headquarters/The Academy and then grungy/dirty industrial mining and factory colonies in the weekly episodes - not a whole lot in between, so the game has a huge gap to fill, creatively - most will enjoy it - some won't. [b]Music/Sound: 9/10[/b] Music: Alex Doty did a great job making this an authentic-sounding Star Trek-style soundtrack without directly lifting/borrowing/stealing already-existing Star Trek themes and melodies. Sound design: The sounds found in the game are a good combination of original and classic Original Series/Strange New Worlds era sound profiles without overdoing it and breaking the immersion. (They didn't just slap things full of stock/nostalgia Star Trek sounds and call it a day) [b]Characters/Story: 8/10[/b] This is probably where I found myself MOST enjoying the game. It is a game with an original story... a Star Trek story. When it comes to Star Trek, the story/characters always matter more than anything else - more than special effects/technology (as 60 years of Trek has taught us.. it's come a LONG way).This is a story with original characters and crew you lead on the journey the game takes you on. The characters felt authentic. Their actions/reactions as the story unfolds seem to come from a place of rational thought and action for those characters. I will admit, there were times the dialogue was a bity clunky - but that wasn't the result of AI, it honestly felt more like a translation misalignment at times (the game studio is not based in the US). Overall, I found myself with a sense of kinship for the officers under my command - at least as much as one can have with digital non-existent characters, heh. Be aware, also, that since this is a game with a discrete storyline, this also has the possibility of affecting [b]'Replaybility'[/b] in a negative way as well - not for all player, but definitely for some, it will. [b]Gameplay: 6/10[/b] This, unfortunately, is where the game in its current state appears to be the weakest. Still well above average, for sure, but easily the weak-link in the whole production - which for many would elicit a "But it's a game, 'gameplay' is the whole reason we're here paying $... why should I pay $ for this?". I will tell you that I personally have enjoyed my gameplay, so far; but the 'objective observer' in me can easily see where some individual players may struggle to enjoy certain aspects of the game, especially where it feels like some of the more obvious QOL features may be missing. Not everything that is slightly-off about things in the game are going to affect every player in the same way - but there's enough 1-off's here and there to eventually catch a majority of players in one way or another. The game does feel a little bit unfinished in some places (some more obvious than others) and I suspect that the dev team was under a strict deadline from Paramount... you know, because the whole "60 Year Anniversary of Star Trek" this year and all. I don't know how much leeway they had to push back any such release deadlines - Paramount is unfortunately quite famous for suddenly pulling plugs on Star Trek projects/game with little to no warning before, during, or even after production. Thankfully that didn't happen here. That, however, also means that the dev team has a bit of work left to do to fully flesh out some of the gameplay in its current state. Thankfully, given the amount of engagement that team has demonstrated both here on Steam™ and over on Discord, I have no reason to suspect that they're going to just quit now because the game has launched. I very much look forward to additional game updates. [h1]The Slightly Deeper Dive[/h1] I'll try to be as spoiler-free as possible, since this IS a game with a storyline. [h2]What this is:[/h2] [b]A true City-builder.[/b] [b]Slower paced.[/b] [b]Not many true 'fail' conditions[/b] - which allows players to explore the new technologies as they become available without risk of 'catastrophic collapse' that would ruin a multi-hour save. [b]Explorable maps[/b] - 1 set map for each planet you will visit - randomized start locations and randomized 'Points of Interest' for each playthrough. [b]A game with a story to tell and characters to introduce[/b] - much like any good Star Trek experience should be. [b]A title with an ACTIVE dev team that has been responsive to feedback.[/b] You can tell from the regular game updates on Steam during development for several months before launch, even though there was no publicly playable game during that time. [h2]What it's NOT:[/h2] [b]Not An RTS[/b] - this is not a fast-paced, high stakes combat sim. Yes, there ARE real (deadly) dangers to your Outpost and crew if you are a careless captain and don't protect them, simply be smart and aware while playing. The story and the city-building are the focus. not the threat of annihilation. [b]Not A.I. slop / Cashgrab[/b] - You get the full game, up front. No paid unlocks, no Day 1 DLC or microtransactions. This isn't a game that was thrown together in a few weeks and launched with no further development - this has been a deliberate and legitimate longtime project, making a deliberate and legitimate faithful 'Star Trek' story. [b]Not Nostalgia-bait:[/b] Not full of stale references to other Star Trek - this is an original story with an original crew(s) - there's a handful of minor cameos that establish the "When" of the game. [b]Not "Woke-Trek"[/b] - it's just 'Star Trek', with a story that could easily have been seen in an episode of 'Strange New Worlds' or 'Voyager'. There is, unfortunately, a very vocal cohort of alleged "fans" (I use the term loosely) who do nothing but yell "woke" and "Nu-Trek" all day everyday these days for any and every Star Trek project made after 2001. This isn't one of those. Feel free to ignore anyone claiming otherwise about this game. You will be able to tell for yourself quite quickly that's it's nothing but a classic-style Star Trek story with classic-style characters doing the story-telling. [h1]Conclusion[/h1] I'm not gonna pretend that this is game doesn't have room for improvement. There are MANY good things going for it, but there are also noticeable things that individual players will expect while playing this game and not find. Not all players will be looking for all things, but there are enough individual players with individual expectations that it will be noticeable on the whole. Thankfully, the Dev team for this game appears to be responsive to feedback during the development phase and there does not appear to be any reason why this title will not continue to receive updates and QOL fixes after launch. I am very much looking forward to those updates!

It would be much nicer if it would be attached to the storyline instead, using only one currency. - The storyline is also quite slow, and somewhat gets neglected at times. - In the whole dynamics of the game, it would have been nice to have the presence of the ship in orbit more involved. E.g. need to find some resource? Perhaps add the option to scan for deposits from orbit once per day, or something like this. Not full map reveal, but just to set markers. - In the lore, teleportation is not possible during tetryon storms, here it is. - The way some of the resources are introduced is very random and artificial: you don't really need water for the crew in the outpost, until you build certain building. Do they just not drink beforehand? The crew in the outpost also doesn't need food until you get a quest to build a mess hall. I mean, sure they probably get it from the ship, but it would be nice to be included in the story, and to make it clear whey this change is made. I think I will drop it for a while, and wait to see if it gets better.

review_text: I've seen some of the negative reviews, but honestly, I don't think the game is nearly as bad as some people make it out to be. Sure, there's room for improvement. I'd love to see more varied terrain, wildlife, plants, creatures, and little storylines to make exploration more interesting. But as it stands, it's a decent base-building game with a day-night cycle, plenty of technology to research, energy and resource management, simple exploration, and a good level of detail. There's definitely potential here. I don't see why a Star Trek fan looking for a Star Trek-themed game wouldn't at least give it a try. I bought it, and so far, I'm enjoying it. I just hope the developers keep working on it, expanding the content, and polishing the rough edges. At its core, it's a building and management simulator. Think of it as a smaller scale SimCity mixed with The Sims, but with a Star Trek atmosphere. You micromanage most of the decisions, oversee your away teams, gather resources, research technology, and work towards building a stable, efficient outpost. It's not trying to be a massive action packed Star Trek adventure, and that's fine. If you enjoy chill base-building, resource management, and the Star Trek universe, there's already a decent amount of fun to be had here. It has a solid foundation. The price is the only issue I have with it, I feel like it should be half the cost. I'll keep it on my list and will be looking forward to seeing how it develops.

review_text: Outposts Unknown is a solid, if slow paced(not in a bad way!), base builder, with a lovely bit of Star Trek flavoring to it. The mechanics of the game are very straightforward for a base builder, nothing is at all obtuse for someone who has only played a handful of games in the genre. Managing your resources is fairly simple, but can be easily screwed up if you aren't paying attention, but even that doesn't have any drastic consequences, at least early on in the game. The Star Trek flavoring is all over the game, from the characters and their interactions, to the theming of all of the base buildings and interactions, anyone who is familiar with or a fan of the series will get a lot of extra joy out of this game. Is the game perfect? No, but it's absolutely worth a chance, and I'm sure the (very) few rough edges I've run into will be polished out in the near future, and those are minor QoL changes. The core game is fantastic.

title: Disney Dreamlight Valley
review_text: **Disney Dreamlight Valley – 5/5 Stars** Disney Dreamlight Valley is pure cozy magic. From the moment you step into the Valley, you’re greeted by familiar Disney and Pixar faces who feel like old friends waiting to welcome you home. The blend of life-sim gameplay, heartfelt storytelling, and endless creative freedom makes this one of the most relaxing and joyful games I’ve played. What really shines is the character interactions. Completing friendship quests with Mickey, Elsa, Moana, and the rest feels meaningful—you’re not just unlocking items, you’re helping restore the Valley and strengthening bonds. The writing captures each character’s personality perfectly, and the little moments of dialogue and animation never fail to make me smile. The gameplay loop is wonderfully balanced. Farming, fishing, cooking, mining, and foraging are all satisfying and feed into both character quests and decorating your dream home and outdoor spaces. The decoration tools are surprisingly deep; I’ve spent hours arranging rooms and outdoor areas just because it feels so good. And every time I think I’ve done it all, a new update or expansion drops and pulls me right back in. It runs smoothly, looks beautiful, and the soundtrack is pure comfort. Whether I’m casually tending my crops while chatting with Goofy or diving into a longer story quest, the game respects my time and never pressures me. It’s the perfect “just one more thing” game that somehow turns into an entire evening of peaceful Disney joy. If you love cozy games, Disney, or simply want a world that feels warm and inviting, Disney Dreamlight Valley is an absolute must-play. Five stars, no question—this one lives on my console permanently.

title: War Thunder
review_text: NICE GAME, WRONG DIRECTION TL;DR: The core gameplay is still fun, but balancing decisions are wildly inconsistent, the modes are getting repetitive even with Nuclear Escalation added, and monetization is aggressive. I still play regularly, but with caveats. I want to say this up front: I enjoy this game and play it often. This review isn't meant to trash, rather, It's meant to point out where I think it's going wrong. GAMEPLAY The core loop works and can be really engaging. The problem is variety. Almost every match comes down to either capturing points or wiping out the enemy team. Nuclear Escalation is the exception, but one mode isn't enough to change how the game feels overall. Air RB is basically team deathmatch on repeat. At high tiers the maps are too small for aircraft to perform the way they were designed to, and there's little reason to play the objectives beyond the SL and RP rewards. Ground RB is the same capture-point formula every time. That's fine on its own, but CAS, inconsistent balancing and heavily compressed BRs make some nations a struggle at certain BRs while others overperform. This is especially bad around the transition from WW2 to Cold War vehicles. Maps are also not up to part especially at higher tiers as they are Small on average very open relative to the spawn points in general not varied BALANCING Balancing decisions, especially around loadouts, don't follow consistent logic. Take the F-14D and the Yak-141. The F-14D still doesn't get the AIM-120, even though it was tested with it. Meanwhile, the Yak-141 received a lot of ordnance it was never planned to carry, purely for balance reasons. If that reasoning works for the Yak-141, it could just as easily apply to the F-14D. this includes balancing of vehicles (i.e. BMPT and T58) MONETIZATION On top of all this, the monetization keeps getting more aggressive. - Launching of premiums at lower br that they should be to clearly push sales - premium needed to avoid terrible maps - stock grind can be really punishing many more aspects WHAT I'D LIKE TO SEE - Air missions built around aircraft roles, such as interception and area denial, so planes actually get to do the jobs they were built for (earl war thunder did it well). - Ground RB modes with real objectives that go beyond capturing points (GHPC is a good example of how this can work). - More historical consistency, especially in Simulator. Lend-lease and copy-paste vehicles don't belong there. There's no reason a Tiger I should have a Japanese M47 on its team in SIM. - less focus on more vehicles being added but a clearly stronger focus on actaully manging the game and it's health - in my eyes infantry is really not needed as enlisted is here for it or at least, it isn't a priorirty until the game health and gameplay loop suffers as such. VERDICT I'll keep playing because deep down I like this game. But I really hope Gaijin moves it in a better direction, starting with the points above.

This game has many mini games, they are nearly independent games, meaning they doesn't have a lot link to each other. Apart from running in the same overall game and having the same characters you can play with, there is little to no link between them. The main issue of why i leave a negative review if this game is good 6 or 7 out of 10 is the size of the game. Right now its 98 Go of final space in your disk (not download space mind you), its one of the heaviest gachas. There is a lot of games that that does what this game does, the only difference they do it better because they only do a little thing that this game does (and take wayyyy less space on your storage). As i said previously, this game is inspired by Yakuza, so if you are here for the story i recommend buying and playing a Yakuza if possible, if not, i hope you know how to sail the seven seas. And if you are here for the mini games, there is a lot how small games that do it better than NTE because they only do that.

title: NTE: Neverness to Everness
review_text: This game has so many negative reviews, and they are all from Hoyoverse no-life fanbase who sit on Reddit all day instead of touching grass, whining about it being a gacha game (point 1) or that the devs use AI to help them continue development (point 2). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Point 1: 1a. Gacha is not a game genre, but a monetization mechanic. You could even call Asphalt Legends a gacha game by this definition, as You are required to pull cars in there aswell. 1b. The monetization practices are WAY less aggressive in NTE than they are in Hoyoverse's slop games. There's also no 50/50s so the limited banner characters are ALWAYS guaranteed, even at the worst luck (90 pulls), although you'll usually get them before that (I've caught up on pulling Lacrimosa this update, because I missed the opportunity in v1.1, I got her at the 70th pull, then a duplicate to upgrade her awakening a few pulls later. All of this was done in 4 days, for free.) Oh, the devs also give players some free resources every major update to help us pull those characters, by the way! Also, remember: You don't have to spend money on these games, if You constantly do, while still hating, You have self-control problems. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Point 2: NTE is NOT the only game that utilizes AI tools to help with game development. Hotta Studio has multiple times clarified the fact, that they do use AI as a helping tool, and they DID mess up a few times where they left AI placeholders in places (they are mostly non-significant textures), where there shouldn't be them, but they quickly fix these issues and remove them. Hoyoverse also uses AI when developing their games, just so you know, yet I haven't seen people complaining. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Conclusion: Neverness to Everness is very entertaining to me, the characters are pleasant to the eye, the world is beautiful, the story and overall concept is good, It runs decent on my low-end, and I like the open-world GTA aspect of it. Don't get me wrong, this game isn't completely perfect, it has flaws and bugs. But it doesn't deserve the hate and doomposting that people give it. We should play games to enjoy them.
